seo.title: Karmic tail 6 20 14 compatibility: love, family and measure
seo.description: Karmic tail 6 20 14 compatibility in the destiny matrix: what The Lovers, Judgement and Temperance mean for a couple, and why this tail is Romeo and Juliet.

title: Karmic tail 6-20-14 in compatibility: Romeo and Juliet's second sonnet
short: The first words Romeo and Juliet say to each other form a sonnet: fourteen lines for two voices, rhymed without either of them planning it. They start a second sonnet straight away and never finish it. The Nurse comes in: "Madam, your mother craves a word with you." That scene holds the whole of the couple's karmic tail 6-20-14: a love that speaks one language from the first minute, a family that walks into the room in mid-line, and a sense of measure the couple still has to learn.

sections.h2: A sonnet for two voices: The Lovers at the entry to the task
paragraphs: The sonnet is one of the strictest forms in English verse: fourteen lines, three quatrains and a couplet, a fixed rhyme scheme. Shakespeare gives the first quatrain to Romeo ("If I profane with my unworthiest hand / This holy shrine, the gentle fine is this"), the second to Juliet, the third they share between them, and the couplet they break in half: one line hers, one his. Two strangers, speaking for the first time, fall into the metre. Quotations from the play are given in Shakespeare's original throughout.

For point M this is an exact picture. In Lisovskaya's reading, the entry of a couple's tail is what the two strive for together: shared wishes, agreements and a "common language". With The Lovers in this place the common language is not built over years; it turns up on the first evening. Such couples recognise themselves in small things: from the first conversation they seem to have known each other for ages; one starts a sentence and the other finishes it; the private jokes arrive before the mutual friends.

The second thing written at the entry is a shared wish. On the balcony Juliet says it in full: "Deny thy father and refuse thy name", "What's in a name? that which we call a rose / By any other name would smell as sweet". The wish of a 6-20-14 couple at the entry is to be two, apart from surnames, from "that's how we do things in our family", from other people's expectations. But point M sits on the line of tasks, and in Lisovskaya the same wish can turn into resistance. The name the two want to throw away at the entry will come back to them, full size, in the middle of the tail.

The third is an agreement given in a single night. Juliet sees the danger herself: "It is too rash, too unadvised, too sudden; / Too like the lightning, which doth cease to be / Ere one can say 'It lightens.'" A few minutes later she sets the terms herself: "If that thy bent of love be honourable, / Thy purpose marriage, send me word to-morrow". The Lovers at the entry to the task are a love that signs before the contract has been read to the end.

And last: this love has no measure, and it is proud of it. "My bounty is as boundless as the sea, / My love as deep; the more I give to thee, / The more I have". At the wedding Juliet is plainer still: "They are but beggars that can count their worth; / But my true love is grown to such excess / I cannot sum up sum of half my wealth." The card of the entry refuses to count. The card of the main task, Temperance, is the art of counting. The whole tail lies between two words: "excess" and "measure".

Benebell Wen writes something about The Lovers that reads like a stage direction for the first scene. When the question is love, the card indicates "the beginnings of romance and, simultaneously, the beginnings of temptation", and "a strong feeling of paradise, at least in the beginning". Romeo and Juliet's first sonnet is written entirely in the words of a church: pilgrims, saints, a shrine, prayer. A 6-20-14 couple's common language at the entry is often the same: lofty, almost sacred, and without a single word yet about housework, money or relatives.

sections.h2: "Your mother craves a word with you": Judgement in the middle of the road
paragraphs: Lisovskaya's key to the twentieth energy in a couple is family and kin: parents, relatives, traditions, inheritance, the influence of the older generation on the union. She gives point N no meaning of its own; for her it simply adds to the main task. We read the middle as a road: what the couple goes through on its way from the wish at the entry to the task at the end. This is the product's reading, not a statement from the book. For the 6-20-14 tail the road runs through two families.

Shakespeare shows it relentlessly: every time the lovers speak to each other, the house interrupts. The second sonnet is cut off by the Nurse with a message from the mother. On the balcony the Nurse calls from inside three times, and three times Juliet answers "anon", without finishing what matters. Then she says the line that holds the whole downside of the middle: "Bondage is hoarse, and may not speak aloud; / Else would I tear the cave where Echo lies" — tear it with "repetition of my Romeo's name".

Judgement is named after the Last Judgement, and the Last Judgement begins with a trumpet: at its sound the dead rise. A trumpet does not whisper. The middle of the 6-20-14 tail demands the same: the union has to sound out loud, before both families. In Shakespeare it never does. The marriage stays a secret of the friar's cell, of two go-betweens — the Nurse and the friar — and of one night. Friar Laurence even has the right plan in his head: "Where thou shalt live, till we can find a time / To blaze your marriage, reconcile your friends, / Beg pardon of the prince, and call thee back". To announce, to reconcile, to call back — that is Judgement at its best: a summons that was answered. Not one point of the plan comes true.

When the family does come in, it comes in as a court. Juliet's father passes sentence the way it is passed in the downside of the twentieth energy: "Speak not, reply not, do not answer me" — and then: "Nor what is mine shall never do thee good". Lisovskaya's list for the downside of this energy describes the same scene almost word for word. Among the couple's difficulties: neither partner can say what they feel. Among its tasks: a union built on the parents' approval or arranged through relatives, and "unaccepted love", when two people love each other but cannot be together because of position or tradition. Among its money troubles: being disinherited. Count Paris, the match planned for Juliet, is a union arranged by the family. The secret marriage to Romeo is the unaccepted love. Both marriages at once are the whole middle of the tail.

The second image of the Last Judgement is the dead rising from their tombs. Shakespeare draws it literally. Juliet, holding the vial, pictures the family vault, "an ancient receptacle, / Where, for these many hundred years, the bones / Of all my buried ancestors are packed", and fears she will wake and "madly play with my forefather's joints". The play never once names the cause of the feud between the Montagues and the Capulets. The Prologue speaks only of an "ancient grudge", and old Montague asks: "Who set this ancient quarrel new abroach?" The past of two families rises from its graves by itself and without explanation. In an ordinary couple this is instantly recognisable: parents' habits, an old grievance of one family against the other, "we have never done it that way" — all of it comes up in the middle of the road, though neither of the two started it.

paragraphs.h3: What the couple's Judgement is made of

paragraphs: The number in the middle of a couple's tail is the sum of the middles of the two personal tails, not recalculated. In 6-20-14 couples neither partner brings Judgement: checking every date since 1900 found no such couple in which either partner has the 20 in their personal tail. The couple's Judgement is always made of two other cards:

Our reading: Shakespeare has all three main pairs. The power of a father whose care "day, night, hour, tide, time, work, play" was "to have her match'd", and the collapse of his house — The Emperor and The Tower. Friar Laurence's rite and the passion he secretly blesses — The Hierophant and The Devil. The prince's sentence and the forty-two hours Juliet spends between life and death — Justice and The Hanged Man. The family's court is made not of wicked people but of ordinary forces: power, tradition, law. What makes them dangerous is only that they meet a secret.

sections.h2: Poison and medicine in one flower: Temperance as the main task
paragraphs: The main point of a couple's tail is D. Lisovskaya reads it mostly through the downside: what is not working for the couple and what it has to learn. For Temperance her list of the couple's tasks includes haste, suppressed emotions, idealisation, dependence on other people's opinions and the wish to control, and among her recommendations are not to jump to conclusions about the partner, to learn to wait for the right moment to act, and to look for the golden mean instead of extremes. In Romeo and Juliet this card has its own voice, and it walks onto the stage with a basket of herbs.

Friar Laurence's first speech is a lecture on Temperance, though the word itself never appears. "The earth that's nature's mother is her tomb; / What is her burying grave that is her womb". And then, about the flower in his hand: "Within the infant rind of this small flower / Poison hath residence and medicine power: / For this, being smelt, with that part cheers each part; / Being tasted, slays all senses with the heart." One and the same substance is medicine or poison; measure decides. The forces that meet in a 6-20-14 couple work the same way: the love of the entry and the family of the middle are neither bad nor good in themselves. What decides is the proportion in which they are mixed. As soon as Romeo walks into the cell he hears from the friar a word of the same root: anyone up at that hour shows "a distemper'd head". Distemper literally means "wrong mixing", from the same Latin temperare as Temperance.

Three scenes later, at the wedding, Laurence states the tail's main task in full: "These violent delights have violent ends", and then, "Therefore love moderately; long love doth so; / Too swift arrives as tardy as too slow." The ending of the play runs exactly by this line. Romeo reaches the tomb too swiftly: he dies minutes before Juliet opens her eyes, and as she kisses him she says, "Thy lips are warm." Friar Laurence arrives too slowly, and his first words in the churchyard are: "how oft to-night / Have my old feet stumbled at graves!" The very friar who warned Romeo: "Wisely and slow; they stumble that run fast."

Everyone in Verona is in a hurry, not only the lovers — and that is an important clue. In the first act Juliet's father tells Paris: "Let two more summers wither in their pride, / Ere we may think her ripe to be a bride." In the third he already fixes the wedding for Thursday and asks himself: "do you like this haste?" Then, delighted by his daughter's apparent consent, he moves it to Wednesday — a day earlier. Because of that shift Juliet takes the potion a day before the friar planned, and his letter to Mantua has a day less to arrive. The letter will fail anyway: its messenger is held in the city because of the plague. Even Laurence hurries at the wedding: "Come, come with me, and we will make short work". Measure is the main task not of one partner, and not only of the two, but of the whole system of two houses.
Shakespeare lays out Lisovskaya's downside of Temperance scene by scene, as if he had read her list:

ul: **a hasty conclusion about the partner** — Romeo hears one sentence from his servant and in the same scene goes to buy poison; the servant begs, "I do beseech you, sir, have patience", and is too late;
**suppressed feelings** — "Speak not, reply not, do not answer me"; Juliet asks her father to "hear me with patience but to speak a word", and that word is never spoken;
**one partner shutting out the family's problems** — Juliet sends the Nurse away and says: "My dismal scene I needs must act alone";
**extremes instead of the middle** — Lady Capulet cuts her husband short: "You are too hot." Wen writes that Temperance comes to "cool what was too hot, heat up what was too cold".

paragraphs: The image worth remembering this play for, Shakespeare keeps for the very end. Juliet wakes and sees in Romeo's hand "a cup", and says: "O churl! drunk all, and left no friendly drop / To help me after?" The couple's main task in 6-20-14 is written in this line in reverse: **do not drink the cup alone**. A decision that concerns two is not taken alone and in one gulp. Why this is precisely Temperance's image shows on Waite's card — more on that below.

Shakespeare opens the second act with a sonnet too, spoken by the Chorus. Its first lines are about a deathbed and an inheritance: "Now old desire doth in his death-bed lie, / And young affection gapes to be his heir". And the fourteenth, the last, runs: "Tempering extremities with extreme sweet". In line fourteen Shakespeare uses the verb of that very card, to temper, and at once shows the counterfeit: one extreme is damped with another. This is the downside of the main task. The Temperance of the 6-20-14 tail is not about sweetening the conflict of two houses with strong feeling; it is about mixing two waters in proportion.

Wen defines the card as "the fusion of two contrasting elements". Writing about work, she adds a thought that fits a couple too: "it isn't that new skills need to be learned, but rather that the Seeker need only reconcile his or her existing skills with the task at hand." A 6-20-14 couple does not need to become different people or give up its families. It needs to blend what each has already brought: two ways of celebrating, two attitudes to money, two styles of quarrelling and making up.

The numbers say the same. In half of 6-20-14 couples (50.9%) Temperance appears in none of the main points of the personal chart — for either partner. Neither of the two brings measure into this union; it appears only when they are together. And the couple's main task is the exact sum, with no folding, of the two personal karmic tasks, most often 4 and 10, 6 and 8, or 3 and 11. The couple's measure is assembled from two different tasks and belongs to neither of them.

sections.h2: Five days instead of nine months: a clue in the history of the plot
paragraphs: Shakespeare had a source: Arthur Brooke's poem The Tragicall Historye of Romeus and Juliet (1562). Its plot is almost the same, with two differences, and both lead to our tail. The poem's editor, J. J. Munro, worked it out in 1908: in Brooke the action stretches over more than nine months, while in Shakespeare it fits into five days — the lovers meet on a Sunday, die on the night of the fifth day, and the play ends on the morning of the sixth. In Brooke, after the secret wedding, the couple has "the summer of their bliss", which lasts "a month or twain"; in Shakespeare, one night. Munro says outright that this compression is the dramatist's own invention. And the second: Brooke's Juliet is sixteen, while Shakespeare's is not yet fourteen.

So the haste in this story was added by Shakespeare. The plot of two feuding families existed before him. He sped it up until time itself became the protagonist of the tragedy. Laurence says "too swift arrives as tardy as too slow", and the play becomes the proof of that line.

Brooke did something else: he judged. In his preface "To the Reader" he explains why the poem was written: to describe "a couple of unfortunate lovers", "neglecting the authority and advice of parents and friends; conferring their principal counsels with drunken gossips and superstitious friars", "abusing the honourable name of lawful marriage to cloak the shame of stolen contracts; finally by all means of unhonest life hasting to most unhappy death". This is Judgement's downside in its purest form: a verdict passed from outside, before the story has been told. Shakespeare lifted that verdict. In his Prologue it is not the children who are to blame but "their parents' strife", and at the end the prince spreads the blame over everyone: "Some shall be pardon'd, and some punished", and earlier, "all are punish'd".

The numbers in the play are coincidences, not clues: Shakespeare knew nothing of the destiny matrix. But they are amusing. In the first act the word "fourteen" is spoken six times, and all six times it is about Juliet's age; when the Nurse asks how long it is until the day she turns fourteen, the mother answers: "A fortnight and odd days." There are three sonnets, forms of exactly fourteen lines, in the play: the Prologue about the two households, the lovers' first exchange, and the Prologue to the second act. And on the night of the balcony Juliet, having agreed to send a messenger to Romeo at nine, sighs: "'tis twenty years till then."

sections.h2: Waite's cards: a trumpet over the tombs and two cups
paragraphs: This section is about the pictures in the classic Waite–Smith deck; the cards on our site differ in their details.

**The Lovers.** Waite calls VI "in all simplicity the card of human love, here exhibited as part of the way, the truth and the life". On the card a man and a woman stand beneath a winged figure, with two trees behind them. For the reversed card Waite gives "Failure, foolish designs". The plan with the sleeping potion, the letter and the flight to Mantua is just such a design, built by a loving heart and a clever friar.

**Judgement.** Waite describes it with a Latin formula: an angel sounds his trumpet "per sepulchra regionum", and the dead arise. It is a line from the medieval hymn Dies irae: "Tuba mirum spargens sonum / Per sepulchra regionum" — "the trumpet, scattering its wondrous sound through the tombs of every land". On the card the trumpet carries a banner with a cross. In the Capulet vault Romeo speaks of banners: "beauty's ensign yet / Is crimson in thy lips and in thy cheeks, / And death's pale flag is not advanced there." The friar had promised Juliet that with the potion "the roses in thy lips and cheeks shall fade / To paly ashes" for a time. Romeo sees the roses have returned and does not grasp what it means: he never received the letter explaining it. The sign of life over the coffin is right before his eyes, and he reads it as a sign of death. Wen calls this the downside of Judgement: misreading the evidence that lay in plain sight. And one more small thing from Waite: he mockingly reports that Court de Gébelin pointed out that "if the grave-stones were removed it could be accepted as a symbol of creation". The middle of the 6-20-14 tail works the same way: the very forces of the family that rise from the tombs become, once the gravestones are gone, the forces from which the couple builds its own life.

**Temperance.** The angel is "pouring the essences of life from chalice to chalice", with "one foot upon the earth and one upon waters". There is drink in both cups at once. In the vault Romeo does the opposite: "drunk all, and left no friendly drop". Waite writes that the card is called Temperance because, when its rule obtains in our consciousness, "it tempers, combines and harmonises the psychic and material natures". And he adds a sentence that ties the main task to the middle: under that rule "we know in our rational part something of whence we came and whither we are going". Whence we came — the two families of the tail's middle. Whither we are going — the couple's shared future. Temperance holds both cups. Even Waite's reversed meaning reads like a stage direction for Shakespeare: "sometimes even the priest who will marry the Querent", and next to it, "disunion, unfortunate combinations, competing interests".

sections.h2: The Sun or the Wheel of Fortune at the couple's centre
paragraphs: The centre of a couple's matrix is the atmosphere of the union, what lies between two people when nobody is watching. 6-20-14 couples have exactly two: The Sun (19) for 53.6% and The Wheel of Fortune (10) for 46.4%.

The Sun never appears at the centre of a personal chart, for any date. It is possible only for a couple, and here it is always made by personal centres 8 and 11 — Justice and Strength, the very two cards Waite swapped. Shakespeare named this atmosphere in one of the most famous lines of the play: "It is the east, and Juliet is the sun. / Arise, fair sun, and kill the envious moon". In Lisovskaya, The Sun at the centre means warmth, respect, family first, closeness. Its downside lists among the tasks an inability to talk about problems and holding feelings back — the same thing as in the downside of Judgement in the middle. A warm atmosphere easily becomes a reason to stay silent: it seems a pity to spoil the sun with a conversation about relatives. The play's last speech is about the same sun: "A glooming peace this morning with it brings; / The sun, for sorrow, will not show his head".

Couples with The Wheel of Fortune at the centre have a different atmosphere. Lisovskaya describes it as the feeling of a fated meeting, and in its downside as a habit of blaming fate and each other. Shakespeare has this too: the "star-cross'd lovers" of the Prologue, Romeo's cry after Tybalt's death, "O, I am fortune's fool!", and his "Then I defy you, stars!" in Mantua. The trap of this atmosphere is calling one's own haste fate.

If the order 6-20-14 stood in one person's personal chart, the centre could only be The Wheel: that personal tail belongs to 484 dates since 1900, and all of them have centre 10. The sunlit atmosphere comes with this tail only for two.

sections.h2: The couple's values: The Empress, The World or The Hanged Man
paragraphs: The couple's values are its spiritual purpose, one more answer to the question of why the two met. 6-20-14 couples have three cards here. The links with the play are our reading.

**The Empress — 49%.** Waite's list for her opens with "Fruitfulness, action, initiative, length of days". Then comes "the unknown, clandestine". And for the reversed card, "public rejoicings". One card holds the whole road Shakespeare's lovers never travelled: from a clandestine wedding to an open celebration and length of days. In Lisovskaya, The Empress means family and marriage, and among the tasks in her downside is getting out from under the influence of one's mother and relatives. The value of these couples is a home of their own that lasts long, not five days.

**The World — 29.8%.** Banished, Romeo tells the friar: "There is no world without Verona walls". The line carries the card's own name. The value of these couples is a world wider than the walls of one city and one family. Shakespeare's ending shows the same card's downside: the Montagues and the Capulets promise to raise statues of the lovers "in pure gold". Waite's reversed World is "Inertia, fixity, stagnation, permanence". A love turned into a monument is The World without movement.

**The Hanged Man — 21.2%.** Waite's list for it includes the word "circumspection" — the very virtue Verona lacked. And the forty-two hours Juliet lies between life and death are the plot's image of The Hanged Man: a halt, a view from the other side, life on pause. The value of these couples is the ability to wait and see a situation differently before acting.

Each point of the couple is the sum of the matching points of two personal charts, folded down to 22. The couple's middle is not recalculated from the couple's entry and task; it too is the sum of the personal middles.
The first date has personal tail 21-4-10 and centre 11. The second has 12-16-4 and centre 8. This is the most common combination of personal tails among 6-20-14 couples: 54% of them.
The couple's centre is 11 + 8 = 19, The Sun. The couple's values are 21, The World. The image of the couple is 10, The Wheel of Fortune.

For this couple the tail's cards stand outside the tail as well. Temperance appears again at "What to create together" (10 + 4 = 14). The Lovers appear three more times: at "What fills" (6 + 18 = 24 → 6), at "Path to prosperity" (15 + 18 = 33 → 6) and at the point "Where it leaks", which on the relationship line is also "Success and the union" (9 + 15 = 24 → 6). Lisovskaya advises adding up repeated energies. Two Temperances give 14 + 14 = 28 → 10, and that is The Wheel of Fortune — exactly the card standing at the couple's "Image of the couple". Our reading: the measure these two are learning on the inside is seen from the outside as their "fate". There is only one Judgement in this matrix: the middle of the tail.

Other combinations of personal tails give the same couple tail less often: 15-5-8 + 9-15-6 for 29% of couples, 15-8-11 + 9-12-3 for 17%, the remaining two under 1%. In 70.4% of 6-20-14 couples neither partner has any of the three cards in their personal tail. A 6 in a personal tail appears only in the second combination (9-15-6) and in the rare fourth, and nobody has Judgement in a personal tail. This tail is almost never brought in by one of the two: the couple puts it together.

sections.h2: The strong version of the tail: how to finish the second sonnet
paragraphs: Romeo and Juliet has a version in which everyone lives. In 1935 Prokofiev wrote a ballet to a scenario by Adrian Piotrovsky and Sergei Radlov with a happy ending: Friar Laurence reaches Romeo in time and explains that Juliet is asleep. Prokofiev put the choice simply: only living people can dance. The ending stirred controversy among Soviet cultural officials, and by the Leningrad premiere of 1940 the tragedy was back. The original score was found in a Moscow archive by the musicologist Simon Morrison, and in 2008 it was danced for the first time, in a production by Mark Morris. The difference between tragedy and happy ending in this story is a few minutes. That is Temperance: not a different love and not different parents, but a different timing.
The strong version of the 6-20-14 tail is a couple that lives the same play slowly. What changes the script:

ul: **Announce the union out loud.** Tell both families what matters in one's own words, not through go-betweens and not after the fact. A Nurse and a friar as the union's only witnesses are the downside of the middle.
**Reread night-time agreements by day.** What was decided on the first evening gets checked in a second, calm conversation.
**Do not judge the partner by a single sentence.** Especially a sentence passed on by a third person.
**Mix the two households in proportion.** Holidays, money, child-rearing, daily routine — agree how much comes from whose house, instead of seizing territory.
**Do not answer "speak not" with silence.** A suppressed feeling in this tail does not vanish; it waits for its vault.
**Do not drink the cup alone.** A decision that concerns two is made by two.

paragraphs: If pressure from relatives turns into threats or violence, it is no longer a task of the tail. Then help is needed: a local emergency number and a psychologist.

The Prologue promises that only the children's death will "bury their parents' strife": only the death of the young could reconcile the two houses. The task of a 6-20-14 couple is to do the same while alive, slowly and with measure. Friar Laurence named it the morning after the first meeting: "this alliance may so happy prove, / To turn your households' rancour to pure love." The strong version of the tail is a couple that finishes the second sonnet, broken off after its first quatrain, and finishes it with the mother already in the room.

ul: **Entry to the task — 6, The Lovers.** The couple enters its task through a shared language found at once, and through a shared wish: to be simply two people, without names and surnames.

**Middle of the task — 20, Judgement.** The road to the main task runs through two families: parents, house rules, old grudges and a past that rises from its graves. The union has to be announced out loud.
**Main task — 14, Temperance.** Learning measure: not deciding everything in one night, mixing two households in proportion, and not drinking the cup alone.

intro: The 6-20-14 tail falls to about one couple in 47, which makes it 15th of the 97 couple tails. It is neither a verdict nor a forecast. Shakespeare's play is this tail lived at a run, in five days, and that is exactly why it shows so clearly where a couple needs measure. What follows is an investigation: what is written in the cards themselves, in the books of Waite, Wen and Lisovskaya, in the history of the plot and in the numbers.

faq.q: What does the karmic tail 6-20-14 mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the tail of the couple's matrix: entry to the task — 6, The Lovers; middle of the task — 20, Judgement; main task — 14, Temperance. The couple enters its task through a shared language and the wish to be two, passes through the meeting with two families, and learns the main thing: measure — not rushing, not deciding for both alone, and mixing two households in proportion.

faq.q: Is the 6-20-14 tail a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail describes a task, not an outcome. It contains no forecast of events or dates: it shows where the union will find things hard and what the two have to learn. Romeo and Juliet is this tail lived at a run; the same story also exists in Prokofiev's version, where the lovers stay alive.

faq.q: How does the couple's tail 6-20-14 differ from the personal tail 6-20-14?
faq.a: A personal tail is calculated from one date of birth, and its points mean different things. A couple's tail is the sum of two personal charts, and its points stand for the couple's shared wishes, the road through its trials and the union's main task. Even with the same numbers it is a different calculation with different roles. The personal tail 6-20-14 always has The Wheel of Fortune at the centre; a couple with this tail has The Sun there in half of cases.

faq.q: How is the 6-20-14 tail calculated in a couple's matrix?
faq.a: Each point of the couple is the sum of the matching points of two personal charts, folded down to 22: entry with entry, middle with middle, task with task. For example, 14.10.1975 and 14.04.1975 give 21 + 12 = 33 → 6, 4 + 16 = 20 and 10 + 4 = 14. The couple's middle is not recalculated from the two outer numbers.

faq.q: Is there a couple tail with 6, 20 and 14 in a different order?
faq.a: No. Among the 97 couple tails these three numbers occur only in the order 6-20-14. The entry of a couple's tail is always a multiple of three, and of the three cards only the 6 meets that condition, while the order 6-14-20 is produced by no pair of dates.

faq.q: What should a 6-20-14 couple do if relatives oppose the union?
faq.a: The tail suggests neither war nor flight, but the slow road of the middle: announce the union directly, in one's own words, ride out the relatives' first reaction, and make no decisions at the peak of emotion. If the pressure turns into threats or violence, it is no longer a task of the tail: help is needed — a local emergency number and a psychologist.

report: The first words Romeo and Juliet say to each other form a sonnet: fourteen lines for two voices, rhymed without either of them planning it. They start a second sonnet straight away and never finish it. The Nurse comes in: "Madam, your mother craves a word with you." That scene holds the whole of the 6-20-14 tail. The Lovers at the entry: a shared language found at once. Judgement in the middle: a family that walks in mid-line. Temperance as the main task: the measure Shakespeare's lovers never had.

report.h3: A love that refuses to count

report: The entry to the task is what the couple wants together, its agreements and its common language. With The Lovers this language is not built over years: from the first conversation the two seem to have known each other for ages, one starts a sentence and the other finishes it. Juliet speaks the shared wish of the entry in full on the balcony: "Deny thy father and refuse thy name". To be simply two people, without surnames and other people's rules. But the entry sits on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance: the name the two throw away on the first evening will come back to them in the middle of the road.

This love has no measure, and it is proud of it. At the wedding Juliet says: "They are but beggars that can count their worth; / But my true love is grown to such excess / I cannot sum up sum of half my wealth." The card of the entry refuses to count. The card of the main task is the art of counting. **The whole tail lies between the words "excess" and "measure".**

The middle of the tail is the road the couple travels from wish to task. With Judgement that road runs through two families: parents, house rules, old grudges. Shakespeare shows it relentlessly: every time the lovers speak, the house interrupts. The second sonnet is cut off by a message from the mother; on the balcony the Nurse calls three times. And Juliet says the line that holds the whole downside of the middle: "Bondage is hoarse, and may not speak aloud".

Judgement is named after the Last Judgement, and the Last Judgement begins with a trumpet. A trumpet does not whisper. **The middle of the 6-20-14 tail demands that the union sound out loud before both families.** In Shakespeare it never does: the marriage stays a secret of the friar's cell, the Nurse and one night. The friar even had the right plan in his head — "To blaze your marriage, reconcile your friends". Not one point of it comes true. When the family does come in, it comes in as a court: "Speak not, reply not, do not answer me". And the play never names the cause of the feud between the two houses: the past rises from its graves by itself and without explanation, the way parents' habits and "we have never done it that way" rise up in any couple.

report.h3: Poison and medicine in one flower

report: Temperance's voice in the play is Friar Laurence with his basket of herbs. His first speech is about a flower in whose "infant rind" both "poison hath residence and medicine power": measure decides. At the wedding he states the tail's main task in full: "Therefore love moderately; long love doth so; / Too swift arrives as tardy as too slow."

The ending runs exactly by this line. Romeo reaches the tomb too swiftly and dies minutes before Juliet opens her eyes: "Thy lips are warm." The friar arrives too slowly, his "old feet stumbled at graves" — the very friar who had warned: "Wisely and slow; they stumble that run fast." Everyone hurries: Juliet's father first wanted to wait "two more summers", then fixed the wedding for Thursday, then moved it to Wednesday. **Measure is the task not of one partner but of the whole system of two houses.**

Shakespeare added this haste to the story himself. In Arthur Brooke's poem, his source, the action stretches over more than nine months; in Shakespeare, five days. Brooke judged the lovers: in his preface they go "hasting to most unhappy death". Shakespeare lifted the verdict and made time the protagonist.

report.h3: Do not drink the cup alone

report: Near the end Juliet sees in Romeo's hand "a cup": "O churl! drunk all, and left no friendly drop / To help me after?" Waite's Temperance angel is "pouring the essences of life from chalice to chalice", so that there is drink in both cups. Romeo drank it all. **A decision that concerns two is not taken alone and in one gulp.**

Shakespeare even named this card's counterfeit. The Prologue to the second act is a sonnet too, and its fourteenth line runs: "Tempering extremities with extreme sweet". The Temperance of a 6-20-14 couple is not about sweetening the conflict of two houses with strong feeling, but about mixing two waters in proportion: two ways of celebrating, two attitudes to money, two styles of quarrelling and making up.

The story also has a version in which everyone lives. In the first scenario of Prokofiev's ballet (1935), Friar Laurence reaches Romeo in time. The difference between tragedy and happy ending is a few minutes: not a different love and not different parents, but a different timing. What changes the script:

ul: announcing the union to both families in one's own words, not through go-betweens;
not judging the partner by a single sentence, especially one passed on by a third person;
mixing the two households in proportion instead of seizing territory;

report: If pressure from relatives turns into threats or violence, it is no longer a task of the tail: help is needed — a local emergency number or crisis line, and a psychologist. The strong version of the tail is a couple that finishes the second sonnet, and finishes it with the mother already in the room.
